At the height of Trump's trade war with China, with tariffs escalating almost weekly, companies like Logitech promptly raised their product prices in the US market significantly.

Earlier this year, the US Supreme Court ruled those tariffs illegal and ordered refunds to manufacturers. However, to date no company has been seen passing the refunds on to consumers, and a class-action lawsuit is now being pursued over this...

Trump's Tariff Saga

Last year, Trump made a big deal about the US trade deficit with China, seemingly fantasising that drastically raising tariffs on Chinese-made products could force companies like Apple to move production back to the US.

Of course, that was never going to happen. The US lacks the manufacturing infrastructure, expertise and cheap labour needed to produce consumer electronics at the scale required by major brands.

Trump kept claiming China would pay the tariffs, but it was actually US brands importing finished goods that paid, and these extra costs were ultimately passed on to consumers in the form of price hikes. At its peak, the tariff rate hit 145%.

Take Logitech as an example — about half of the company's product lines saw price increases of up to 25%.

Consumers Deserve Refunds

The US Supreme Court ultimately ruled that Trump had no authority to impose those tariffs unilaterally, and ordered refunds to be paid to US businesses. The refund process is currently underway.

The problem is that the costs were ultimately borne by consumers through higher prices, but so far none of the affected companies have signalled any plans to refund their customers.

Law firm CPM has filed a class-action lawsuit against Logitech over this, seeking refunds for consumers who paid higher prices during the period the tariffs were in effect.

9to5Mac's Take

The logic here is indisputable. Businesses paid the tariffs, passed the extra cost on to consumers, and now the government is refunding the businesses. From a moral standpoint, those businesses should pass that money back to the consumers who bought products during that period.

In practice, though, this would be extremely difficult to execute. Logitech would need to identify all relevant transactions across its vast network of third-party retailers, track what consumers paid, and calculate what portion of that was attributable to the tariffs.

If this lawsuit ultimately succeeds, it could set a very interesting precedent — though it's worth noting that in class actions, the main beneficiaries tend to be the lawyers, and the amounts individual consumers actually receive are usually tiny.
